slot.brief: Why are Zn2+, Sc3+ or Cu+ salts colourless while Cu2+ is blue — d-d transitions and d-electron count.

stem: Why are salts of $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ generally colourless, whereas salts of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ are often coloured?
options: $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has a filled $d^{10}$ subshell, while $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ has a partially filled $d^9$ subshell that permits $d$–$d$ transitions.
Both ions have partially filled $d$ subshells, but $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has a larger atomic radius.
$\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has a partially filled $d$ subshell, while $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ has a filled $d^{10}$ subshell.
Both ions have filled $d$ subshells; the colour of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is due to $s$–$p$ transitions.

verdicts.working: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, so it has no d–d transitions; Cu²⁺ is d⁹, allowing d–d transitions that often produce colour.

working:
$\text{Zn}^{2+}:[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$; no partially filled $d$ subshell for $d$–$d$ transitions.\n$\text{Cu}^{2+}:[\text{Ar}]3d^9$; $d$–$d$ transitions can absorb visible light.

Independent check: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, so it has no d–d transitions; Cu²⁺ is d⁹, allowing d–d transitions that often produce colour.
solution:
$\text{Zn}^{2+}:[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$ has a filled $d$ subshell and no $d$–$d$ transitions.
$\text{Cu}^{2+}:[\text{Ar}]3d^9$ has a partially filled $d$ subshell, allowing $d$–$d$ transitions that can absorb visible light and produce colour.
